fixes.explanation: Sending Leah back to her father isn't in this verse, friend. Verse 31 says, “When the LORD saw that Leah was unloved, He opened her womb…” The LORD sees her first, and then He acts. Going home isn't the action the text gives.

You got it, baker. When Judah is born, Leah says, “This time I will praise the LORD.” With Levi she spoke about her husband becoming attached to her (Genesis 29:34). With Judah she says she will praise the LORD, and I think that's worth noticing.
Not this time, baker. Verse 35 says it plainly: “Then Leah stopped having children.” Judah is her fourth son, and no baby comes right after him. Four sons is the count at that point.

Right. Genesis 29:35 says, “Then Leah stopped having children.” Judah is her fourth son, and the text says she stopped after him. No baby comes right after Judah. Four sons is where the count stands at that point.

That's the one. The text says Rachel envied her sister, and then she says to Jacob, “Give me children, or I will die!” No hints and no warm-up, just straight to the point. I think Jacob felt that one.

Sending Leah away isn't what Rachel asks for, friend. The text says she envied her sister, and then she tells Jacob, “Give me children, or I will die!” Her request is about children. Envy is the feeling the text names.

Leah's name never comes up in Jacob's answer, friend. Rachel has just spoken to him, and he says, “Am I in the place of God, who has withheld children from you?” The word he lands on is God. I think that was a tense moment between those two.

Verse 9 says Leah gave her servant Zilpah to Jacob as a wife. Asking Rachel for Bilhah isn't in the text, friend. Bilhah is Rachel's servant, and Leah has a servant of her own. Zilpah is the name to remember.

Jacob going back to Rachel isn't what the text gives, baker. Genesis 30:9 says Leah saw that she had stopped having children, and she gave her servant Zilpah to Jacob as a wife. That's her move. Zilpah is the name to hold on to.
Foolish isn't the word, friend. Leah says, “How happy I am! For the women call me happy.” The word the women use is happy. That's why she names this son Asher.

Not quite, baker. Genesis 30:14 says Reuben found mandrakes in the field during the wheat harvest and brought them to his mother. His mother is Leah, so the mandrakes go to Leah first. Rachel is the one who then asks Leah for some.

Right. Genesis 30:14 says Reuben found mandrakes in the field and “…brought them to his mother…” His mother is Leah, so the mandrakes go to Leah, not Rachel. Then Rachel begs Leah, “Please give me some of your son’s mandrakes.”

That's what Rachel offers. In Genesis 30:15 she says, “he may sleep with you tonight in exchange for your son’s mandrakes.” The “he” is Jacob, so the trade is a night with him for the mandrakes. Leah had just asked, “Is it not enough that you have taken away my husband?” I think this one is a tense trade.

Right. Genesis 30:17 says, “And God listened to Leah, and she conceived and bore a fifth son to Jacob.” That's Issachar, so after that night Leah does have another son. A sixth son comes after him, and then a daughter. Her family keeps growing, baker.
That's right. In the same verse where she names Joseph, Rachel says, “May the LORD add to me another son.” Her words right after his name are a request for one more boy. I think that's hope, baker.
